title: Ursinus: reigning sin singularly mortal; non-reigning singularly venial
source_text: XXVIII. Sed sunt adhuc qui distinctionem peccati in mortale & veniale alio sensu sumunt. Nam Zacharias Ursinus in Explicationibus Catecheticis, & David Paraeus qui illas recognovit, dicunt peccatum regnans singulari modo mortale, peccatum vero non regnans singulari modo veniale dici posse. Et sic peccatum mortale est cui peccans non resistit per gratiam Spiritus Sancti, & propter quod fit, actu & reipsa, morti aeternae obnoxius. Cujusmodi sunt in renatis ipsis lapsus contra conscientiam, cum quibus fiducia remissionis peccatorum, & consolatio vera non consistit, donec resipiscant. Veniale vero cui peccans resistit per gratiam Spiritus Sancti, & propter quod, Deo miserante, non fit actu morti aeternae obnoxius. Cujus generis peccata sunt, Omnes inclinationes & cupiditates pravae, & multa peccata ignorantiae, omissionis & infirmitatis, reliquiae in sanctis, quamdiu sunt in hac vita, quae tamen agnoscunt, deplorant, & oderunt, & in quibus etiam fidem & consolationem retinent, ut habet locus jam ex Ursino citatus, titulo De Peccato actuali.
pass_a_gloss: But there are still those who take the distinction of sin into mortal and venial in another sense. For Zacharias Ursinus in the Catechetical Explications, and David Paraeus who revised them, say that reigning sin can be called mortal in a singular way, but non-reigning sin venial in a singular way. And so mortal sin is that which the sinner does not resist by the grace of the Holy Spirit, and on account of which he becomes, in act and in very deed, liable to eternal death. Of which kind in the regenerate themselves are falls against conscience, with which confidence of the remission of sins and true consolation do not stand until they repent. But venial is that which the sinner resists by the grace of the Holy Spirit, and on account of which, God having mercy, he does not become actually liable to eternal death. Of which kind of sins are all wicked inclinations and desires, and many sins of ignorance, omission, and infirmity, remains in the saints so long as they are in this life, which nevertheless they acknowledge, bewail, and hate, and in which they also retain faith and consolation, as the place already cited from Ursinus has it, under the title On actual sin.
pass_b_english: Ursinus/Paraeus: call reigning sin singularly mortal—the unresisted, actually death-liable fall against conscience.
Non-reigning remains singularly venial: Spirit-resisted infirmities where faith and comfort still dwell.
